https://www.dailysabah.com/politics/turk.text: Politics Diplomacy Legislation War On Terror EU Affairs Elections News Analysis Turkish F-16 fighter jets gear up for key Baltic mission by Daily Sabah with Agencies ISTANBUL Jul 26, 2026 - 2:53 pm GMT+3 A F-16 fighter jet takes off for a training mission, Diyarbakır, southeastern Türkiye, July 26, 2026. (AA Photo) by Daily Sabah with Agencies Jul 26, 2026 2:53 pm Five F-16 fighter jets and 76 crew members will soon fly to Estonia as the Turkish air force prepares to undertake an air policing mission in the Baltic region as part of a NATO operation. The jets and their personnel continue preparations for the important task, which comes amid heightened concerns about the risk of the Russia-Ukraine conflict spilling over into the region. Also known as the “Pars (Leopard) Squadron,” the unit is currently based at its home base in Diyarbakır, southeastern Türkiye. Key NATO ally Türkiye often offers its services for the alliance’s air policing missions in Europe. This time, the squadron will be stationed at Amari Air Base in Estonia, which does not have its own fighter jets, unlike the other Baltic countries, Lithuania and Latvia. The crews will be in Estonia from August to November for round-the-clock Quick Reaction Alert missions, keeping watch for airspace violations. F-16 fighter jets fly above Diyarbakır, southeastern Türkiye, July 26, 2026. (AA Photo) The squadron’s commander, Lt. Col. Özdemir, told Anadolu Agency (AA) on Sunday that air policing is a peacetime air defense activity. “It is strategically important for the defense of NATO’s eastern flank. It will make important contributions to Türkiye, particularly by strengthening international deterrence, promoting joint operations with allied forces and helping them enhance their strategic capabilities,” he said. He noted that the 181st Jet Squadron Command, to which Pars belongs, is one of the oldest and largest strike forces in eastern Türkiye. Özdemir said their mission would mainly consist of monitoring airspace violations and responding to unidentified aerial vehicles. “Pars is a squadron that has repeatedly proven itself in both domestic and international missions. We are confident that we will perform this task in the best possible way and represent Türkiye in the Baltic skies,” he added. First Lt. Özmen, a member of the squadron, said the Turkish Air Force ranks above its peers thanks to tough, disciplined and continuous training. Pilots hold their helmets before they board the fighter jets, Diyarbakır, southeastern Türkiye, July 26, 2026. (AA Photo) “This is certainly not solely the success of pilots. Behind all our accomplishments are crews, from maintenance workers to air traffic controllers, from planning officers to backup personnel, who devote their lives to these missions and demonstrate a strong team spirit,” Özmen said. Under NATO’s Baltic Air Policing mission, the security of the Baltic skies has been provided by NATO member countries since 2004, when Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania joined the alliance. NATO member countries with the necessary capabilities voluntarily contribute to the Baltic Air Policing mission, with responsibility rotating every four months. Since the mission was first deployed in 2004, participating NATO fighter jets have been stationed at Siauliai Air Base in Lithuania. Since 2014, NATO aircraft have also been deployed at Amari Air Base in Estonia, while they have also been able to operate from Lielvārde Air Base in Latvia since 2024. As part of NATO’s Air Policing mission, the Turkish Air Force successfully completed Enhanced Air Policing missions in Poland from July 6 to Sept. 15, 2021, and in Romania from Nov. 30, 2023, to April 2, 2024. Türkiye is also scheduled to take on the air policing mission in Romania from December 2026 to March 2027. shortlink copied KEYWORDS nato air policing turkish air forces squadron f-16 fighter jets The Daily Sabah Newsletter Keep up to date with what’s happening in Turkey, it’s region and the world. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text: Rumen Radev during the April elections, where his Progressive Bulgaria party secured an overwhelming majority. Photograph: Spasiyana Sergieva/Reuters View image in fullscreen Rumen Radev during the April elections, where his Progressive Bulgaria party secured an overwhelming majority. Photograph: Spasiyana Sergieva/Reuters Bulgaria Is Bulgarian prime minister Rumen Radev sizing up the EU’s Orbán-shaped hole? Rightwing populist’s inconsistent positions on Europe and Russia suggest he is testing how far he can push partners and electorate Eden Maclachlan in Sofia Wed 19 Aug 2026 06.47 EDT Last modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 08.26 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google O ne evening nine years ago in the Bulgarian town of Balgari, a Brazilian tourist approached the casually dressed, middle-aged man surrounded by bodyguards, bystanders and photographers. “ Why are you important? ” she asked. “I’m not so important,” he replied. She repeated the question and he admitted: “I’m the president.” Now, in 2026, the rightwing populist Rumen Radev is no longer the president, but the prime minister – the more powerful of the two positions – after his Progressive Bulgaria party secured an overwhelming majority in April’s election. While many in Europe breathed a sigh of relief that month at the demise of Viktor Orbán in Hungary, others wondered if Radev would become the EU’s next disruptor-in-chief. His first months, analysts suggested, have pointed towards a more transactional foreign policy with the US and Europe , and some initial moves that could be seen to benefit Russia. In May, Bulgaria halted its military support to Kyiv, with Radev saying he believed the Ukrainian cause was “doomed”. When 36 countries signed up to a special tribunal to prosecute Russia over its invasion of Ukraine, Bulgaria did not. Visiting Paris on Bastille Day, Radev pulled Bulgaria out of the “coalition of the willing”, saying his country does not have the capacity to help Ukraine , and that military support will only prolong the war. View image in fullscreen Rumen Radev (left) meeting the French prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, and the first lady, Brigitte Macron, for the Bastille Day military parade in Paris on 14 July. Photograph: Jeanne Accorsini/Sipa/Shutterstock Days later, Bulgaria agreed to host up to eight US aerial refuelling tankers at the Bezmer military base to support US operations in the Middle East. “He’s already an awkward leader for Europe because his moves are surprising Europeans by the fact that Bulgaria, for many years, despite its internal challenges, held its pro-European course,” said Maria Simeonova, the head of the Sofia office at the European Council on Foreign Relations. View image in fullscreen Maria Simeonova: ‘Orbán’s actions had consequences for the EU and Hungary, whereas Radev’s actions will only have consequences for Bulgaria.’ Photograph: Eden Maclachlan She said Radev, while maintaining Bulgaria’s commitment to the EU and Nato, was distancing the country from the emerging European security architecture yet hoping to continue benefiting from US security guarantees. “There’s clearly a lack of any ideological consistency in the way he conducts foreign policy in those first months,” she said. “And this is becoming very visible now.” Meanwhile, the prime minister, who had never previously expressed any strong views about his faith, religion or the church, has now found an affinity with Orthodox Christianity. In June, Progressive Bulgaria supported the March of the Family, a Christian and patriotic event supporting traditional family values defined as being in direct opposition to Sofia Pride, which happened on the same day. Radev also threatened to veto the EU’s 21st package of sanctions against Russia over its war against Ukraine, which included measures against the head of the Russian Orthodox Church, Patriarch Kirill. “I am not interested in the Russian patriarch as an individual,” Radev told reporters. “I am interested in the fact that he is the head of the Russian Orthodox Church, which is Eastern Orthodox, just like our church. I am concerned about the millions of people who belong to that church.” A source close to the Bulgarian Orthodox Church, speaking on condition of anonymity to preserve its relationship with the patriarch, said Radev’s recent rapprochement with the church was purely political. “He doesn’t have anything to do with the church and religion. It is 100% political,” they said. “I think it was just a gesture towards Moscow. It has no practical benefit for Bulgaria, nor for Radev.” Dimitar Keranov, a visiting fellow at the German Marshall Fund of the US, said Radev was “sitting on two chairs” with pro-European and pro-Russian statements in an attempt to appease his diverse electorate. However, he said, this tactic would not prevail. “There’s this idiom in Bulgarian: He who sits on two chairs falls,” said Keranov. “My opinion is that if he continues this, sooner or later it will turn against him.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion View image in fullscreen Vladislav Bonev: ‘It would be good to have Radev kept in check by the EU.’ Photograph: Eden Maclachlan Vladislav Bonev, 19, an IT student at Sofia University, said he was disappointed with the government and that the pro-Russia rhetoric was not showing Bulgaria in a good light to other European leaders. Yet, he said, he was not too concerned about the possibility of Radev pulling Bulgaria out of the EU and Nato. “I don’t think we have anything to worry about because he doesn’t have that much power to pull us out of the EU,” he said. “But what would be good is to have him kept in check by the EU.” It is too early to determine whether Radev is emerging as the new Orbán. Simeonova said she believed Radev, who does not see the EU as a solidarity club, would not be as disruptive or block crucial EU decisions. But some of his actions may have dire consequences for the country and prevent its development. “The difference with Orbán, is that Orbán’s actions had consequences for the EU and Hungary, whereas Radev’s actions will only have consequences for Bulgaria, marginalising the country, isolating the businesses from any opportunities,” she said. Keranov said Radev lacked the infrastructure to be as disruptive as Orbán. He said he believed, however, that Radev could yet become a more awkward leader for Europe. “If he is given enough time, like Orbán was given as prime minister, we could expect him consolidating his power more and more, blocking some reforms that are not really in his interest, or even turning this pro-Russian rhetoric into even more pro-Russian policy in practice,” he said. “We need to be aware that, right now, he’s also just testing the ground.” Nevertheless, some believe Radev will face some serious problems in the autumn once Bulgarians are back from their holidays. A newly approved budget, freezing the minimum monthly wage at €620.20, projecting a 5.7% GDP deficit, and authorising up to €10.1bn in new government borrowing, has considerably rattled part of the electorate. Last December, the proposed state budget for 2026 provoked mass protests, resulting in the resignation of the then prime minister, Rosen Zhelyazkov, and his cabinet . Tsvetelina Mareva, 27, who runs a children’s centre in Sofia, said she was disappointed about Radev’s pro-Russia stance and wished he was focusing on his campaign promises. “We can see now that he lied to us,” she said. “So probably we’ll go to protest after the summer. We are already talking about that on social media. In September I am sure there will be a lot of protests.” Explore more on these topics Bulgaria European Union Russia Ukraine Europe news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

Share it with your friends! Facebook Twitter Google Pinterest Reddit Email LinkedIn The Bucharest Court of Appeal rejected the accusations of human trafficking and organized criminal group made against Viorel Pașca, the owner of an authorized care homes network in Bihor County, western Romania, when it ruled against his detention back in July. The information emerged from the reasoning of the judge, now made public, who decided on July 16 that Viorel Pașca and his family members should be investigated while at liberty, an opinion contrary to that of the other magistrate from the Bucharest Tribunal who considered that “there are reasonable suspicions” against Pașca. “At least at first glance”, the manner in which the injured persons were treated in Pașca’s nursing homes “does not present characteristic elements of keeping persons in a state of slavery or subjecting them to procedures similar to deprivation of liberty or servitude,” the Court of Appeals judge said, according to Digi24 . DIICOT prosecutors had said that the victims were treated improperly, and that money intended for their care did not serve the stated purpose. However, the judge rejected DIICOT’s accusations. The sums of money were not appropriated by Pașca and his family, according to the evidence presented. The Bucharest Court of Appeal also maintained that “the accommodated persons benefited from basic medical assistance.” Those in the care homes had “periodic medical consultations, including psychiatric specialist consultations, from prescribed and monitored treatments, from recreational activities and from assistance in carrying out current activities.” The judge further mentioned that “persons with mental illnesses were involved in various activities carried out within the community and benefited from bodily hygiene services - haircuts, washing, shaving, as well as clean clothing and linen.” Among deficiencies, the Court noted the fact that the persons dealing with the care of the sick and the administration of medicines had an extremely low educational level. Some did not have the ability to read and write. Similarly, several accommodated persons did not benefit “in all situations” from “the medical treatment corresponding to the illnesses they suffered from.” Moreover, some of the patients contributed to the administration of medicines. The staff dealing with the care of the elderly was insufficient; However, these shortcomings, the judge of the Bucharest Court of Appeal maintained, are due to “the lack of financial resources, and not at all to the fact that the defendants appropriated the money from which the patients benefited from the received donations.” At the same time, the judge further said that the aid received from the state by vulnerable persons (such as a pension or any other form of social assistance) would not have allowed them to live in better conditions than those ensured by Viorel Pașca’s family. The Bihor illegal care homes case broke at the end of June, uncovering similarities with another, more serious case from 2023 . Unlike the latter, however, the situation of the care homes in Bihor is not as clear, leading many to argue that Viorel Pașca and his association were doing their best with the available resources, taking care of patients who had been abandoned by state institutions. Ever since then, Viorel Paşca defended the activity of his association, which housed vulnerable people despite the fact that it lacked a license to do so. radu@romania-insider.com (Photo source: stavrio | Dreamstime.com ) Read next 22 July 2026 Healthcare CoE Commissioner for Human Rights expresses concern over illegal care homes case in Romania Normal Justice Bucharest Court of Appeals gives reasoning in Bihor unauthorized care homes case 11 August 2026 Radu Dumitrescu Like this article? https://www.politico.eu/article/nigel-fa.text: LONDON — Nigel Farage’s critics have long accused him of having a weakness on Vladimir Putin. Now Reform UK wants to tee up a visit to Ukraine. Two party officials told POLITICO on Monday that discussions have been held between the party and Ukrainian contacts about the prospect of a trip for the Reform leader. Farage’s opponents often hurl at him comments he made back in 2014 that he “admired” the Russian president as an “operator.” Then, a decade later, he triggered a mid-general election backlash by claiming it was the West that “ provoked ” Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine. Advertisement Advertisement The imprisonment of Reform’s former Wales leader last year for taking Russian bribes has only added to perceptions that Farage has a “Putin problem.” Polling carried out by More in Common last year suggests that while every voting group in Britain overwhelmingly backs Ukraine, only 26 percent believe that Farage feels the same. Some 21 percent reckon he sympathizes more with Russia. But Reform hopes it could go some way to dispelling that perception by arranging for Farage to visit Ukraine. “I know it’s been discussed,” said a first official, whose comment was backed up by a second official. Both were granted anonymity to discuss plans yet to be finalized. Neither could say at what level the talks have been held. Reform declined to comment, as did the Ukrainian Embassy. The first official said they believe a visit could go some way to dispelling the impression Farage has any sympathy for Putin — but warned a visit could “piss off a lot of our members.” Advertisement Advertisement Separate research by Opinium last year suggests that Reform voters are significantly more skeptical about continued British support for Ukraine than backers of other parties. Should the visit go ahead, it would mark the latest attempt from Farage to distance himself from his past statements. In October, he called Putin “a very bad dude” and said the U.K. should shoot down Moscow’s jets that enter British airspace. The most maximalist ambition for a visit to Kyiv would be a meeting with Volodymyr Zelenskyy himself, though officials declined to comment on whether that prospect had been discussed. Guidance from the Foreign Office, which isn’t facilitating parliamentarian travel to Ukraine, warns against any travel to most of Ukraine because of the assessed risk to British nationals. A Whitehall official pointed out this advice applies to MPs as well as regular Brits. It would not be unheard of for opposition leaders to visit the Ukrainian president: Keir Starmer did it while Rishi Sunak was prime minister in 2023. Reform has been arranging a series of visits, due to take place later this year, with international allies, including Marine Le Pen , the president of France’s far-right National Rally party. Advertisement Advertisement Le Pen would be French president if she wins next year’s elections. Jordan Bardella, who played a big role in Reform’s party conference in Birmingham last weekend, would be her pick for prime minister. Reform has been making a point of engaging with Kyiv’s representatives, and the Ukrainian Embassy in London sent a representative to this year’s Reform UK conference. Esther Webber contributed to this report.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckn9.text: Image source, Reuters Image caption, The blast occurred at a mosque building near police headquarters By Usman Zahid ,Â Reporting from Islamabad ,Â AndrÃ© Rhoden-Paul Â and Â Ella Kipling Published 18 September 2026, 11:13 BST Updated 3 minutes ago A car-bomb attack on a mosque at a police compound in north-western Pakistan has killed at least 21 people and injured more than 100, officials say. Fifteen police officers and a four-year-old child are among those killed in the suicide attack, which also involved gunmen firing on the police facility in the city of Kohat in the province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan's APP news agency reported. Video found by BBC Verify shows the site covered in rubble and people tending to casualties. Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Police suggested a faction of the Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), also known as the Pakistani Taliban, carried out the attack. A car loaded with explosives rammed into the entrance of the mosque at about 13:15 local time (08:15 GMT), police say. Friday prayers were taking place at the time. At least six of the attackers were killed in the explosion and the gun battle that followed, according to a Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Police spokesperson. In a post on X, the force said it was "determined to foil the nefarious designs of Fitna-al-Khawarij" - the designation used by officials to refer to the Pakistani Taliban. The group was set up in 2007 with the aim of enforcing its strict version of Islamic law and is allied with al-Qaeda and the Afghan Taliban. Pakistan's President Asif Ali Zardari expressed "his best wishes for the swift recovery of those injured in the explosion" in a statement, and called for the "complete elimination" of foreign-backed terrorists. Image source, EPA A UN spokesman said Secretary-General AntÃ³nio Guterres "strongly condemns" the bombing and that "attacks targeting civilians and places of worship are unacceptable". In February, officials accused the Pakistani Taliban of being behind a series of attacks in the country, including the suicide bombing of a Shia mosque in Islamabad in which more than 30 people were killed. Faisal Karim Kundi, governor of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, said on Friday the province had endured "immense sacrifices in the fight against terrorism". Militancy in Pakistan's border areas has risen sharply in recent months, with armed groups targeting the military and police. Islamabad says militants use Afghanistan as a safe haven to train and plan attacks in Pakistan. Afghanistan's Taliban government denies the accusation and says militant groups are a domestic problem for Pakistan. https://witl.com/ixp/691/p/legs-inn-cros.text: Legs Inn Celebrates 100 Years: Cross Village, Emmet County Legs Inn Celebrates 100 Years: Cross Village, Emmet County John Robinson John Robinson Published: September 22, 2026 Offered by mc2-treasures via ebay Share on Facebook Share on Twitter I have been by this place many times over the years and finally decided to find out something about it. It’s Legs Inn, located at 6425 Lakeshore Drive in Cross Village. Polish immigrant Stanley Smolak arrived in Northern Michigan during the 1920s and attempted to find somewhere that was reminiscent of his hometown in Poland. It also needed to be a place where he could practice his talent of making wood sculptures. Get our free mobile app Stanley loved living in this area among the Native Americans and nearby a stove manufacturing company. He also was fascinated with the large rocks along (and in) Lake Michigan. It was his love of wood and rocks that brought about the construction of Legs Inn. The structure became a combination of his Polish heritage and his love of Northen Michigan. Why was his place called “Legs” Inn? It was the hundreds of cast iron stove legs that he placed along the roof line that made a parapet, therefore becoming known as ‘Legs’ Inn. Construction began in the 1920s with consistent upgrading through the 1940s. It became a combination of museum and Polish restaurant with living quarters, gift shop, and saloon. After his wife passed in 1968, Stanley died six months afterward. Legs Inn remains in the family and achieved historic status in 1989. Photograph: Charlie Riedel/AP Health Abortion pill access jumps almost 50% after Australia eases restrictions for pharmacies The number of pharmacies stocking the MS-2 Step medication increased from 2,228 to 4,107 after rules relaxed in 2023 Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Melissa Davey Medical editor Wed 7 Oct 2026 11.00 EDT Last modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 16.31 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The number of Australian pharmacies stocking an abortion pill increased by almost 50% when prescribing restrictions were relaxed, with researchers saying the findings suggest deregulation of abortion promotes safer and faster healthcare. A study published in the medical journal JAMA Network Open on Thursday examined the impact of changes by the Therapeutic Goods Administration in 2023 which meant the medication, MS-2 Step, could be prescribed by any GP. Prior to the changes, GPs needed additional training and registration to prescribe it. The requirement for pharmacists to be registered to dispense the drug was also scrapped, and administrative hurdles were relaxed. Appropriately trained nurse practitioners and endorsed midwives also became eligible prescribers. Women suffer more pain than men across the whole body, major global study finds Read more By comparing pharmacy ordering data in the two years before and after the changes, researchers led by La Trobe University found by mid-2025, 49% more pharmacies were stocking the medication. There were 2,228 pharmacies stocking it before the policy change, rising to 4,107 by mid-2025. The number of postcodes with a pharmacy stocking the medication rose from 915 to 1,292 – or nearly half of all Australian postcodes – two years after the changes. Regional coverage increased from 23% to 35% of postcodes, while the proportion of stocking pharmacies in remote areas nearly doubled, rising from 12.5% to 22%. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email The lead author of the paper, Prof Kristina Edvardsson from La Trobe University’s School of Nursing and Midwifery, said it showed “Australian women who need access to this medication can access it closer to home”. “It removes the unnecessary travel and stress around getting the medication once it’s prescribed. That’s super important, particularly for women who might be more disadvantaged, women living in rural, remote areas, and women who might not have the means to travel. “If you can go to your local pharmacy and pick up this medication, it means getting care quicker.” Edvardsson said other studies have found improving access to MS-2 Step is safe, and that when access to the medical abortion pill increases , the need for surgical abortion decreases. “In some European countries, medical abortion accounts for more than 90% of all abortions, and it looks like we’re heading that way here as well with a steady increase in medication abortion versus surgical abortion,” she said. MS-2 Step, available under the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme, comprises two drugs used together, mifepristone and misoprostol . It can be taken until up to 63 days of gestation. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion At the time of the study, MS-2 Step was the only abortion pill available, but in February an additional drug, Arzestra, comprising the same two medicines, was approved by the TGA . Dr Anna Noonan, a postdoctoral research fellow and abortion researcher with the University of Technology Sydney, said the data should be “an important signal” to countries where more restricted prescribing was still in place, such as the US. “There are still pervasive, unnecessary barriers in lots of places, and data like this is an important signal that regulation and overregulation is not the way forward,” she said. Noonan said there was still work to be done to improve rural and regional access, and that her own research suggested a lot of “invisible work” also occurred by local doctors, nurses and advocates working behind the scenes so that people can confidentially and more easily find healthcare. “Doctors and nurses are going to pharmacies in advance saying, ‘I’m going to be an abortion provider in this community, will you stock this medication?’ “Overregulation creates extra work for those trying to provide timely care, and it doesn’t work out in the best interests of people seeking care,” Noonan said. “The more we encourage a deregulated environment, the easier access will be, particularly for people with less resources.” Explore more on these topics Health Women's health Abortion news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Victorian Labor makes abortion access easier amid fears One Nation could try to wind it back Women suffer more pain than men across the whole body, major global study finds One Nation senator Malcolm Roberts says he will push for party to adopt blanket abortion ban An ‘onslaught of punches’: is this week the cost-of-living tipping point for many Australian households? Newsflash Newsroom , 02.10.2026, 20:00 CONSULTATIONS – Romanian President Nicușor Dan will invite the presidents and representatives of the political parties and formations represented in Romania’s Parliament on Monday for consultations on the nomination of a candidate for the post of prime minister, the Presidential Administration said in a statement on Friday. According to the statement, the talks will begin with the Social Democratic Party (PSD), the Alliance for the Union of Romanians (AUR) and the National Liberal Party (PNL), and will conclude with unaffiliated MPs. Nicușor Dan has asked the parties to come to the consultations with viable solutions. He has ruled out AUR being part of a new government, explaining that this would affect Romania’s relations with its partners, and has assured that the country’s pro-Western direction will be maintained and that its financial commitments will be honored. The president has already announced that he will nominate a new prime minister on Monday, at the end of the talks. Romania’s Parliament in Bucharest failed to give a vote of confidence on Wednesday to the government proposed by Liberal MEP Siegfried Mureșan. It is the second government to fail to secure parliamentary approval, following that of Liberal politician Adrian Veștea in June. It has been almost five months since the PSD and AUR brought down the government led by Liberal Ilie Bolojan in May through a motion of no confidence. CASE – Romania’s interim prime minister, Liberal politician Ilie Bolojan, was questioned as a witness on Friday at the National Anticorruption Directorate (DNA) office in Iași, north-eastern Romania, in a case in which a businessman is accused of incitement to blackmail and influence peddling. Prosecutors wanted details about a meeting the prime minister had with businessman Fănel Bogos at the government headquarters in September last year. Bogos is suspected of having paid for the meeting and of trying to persuade Bolojan to dismiss the head of the Vaslui Veterinary and Food Safety Directorate in eastern Romania. The businessman is alleged to have been unhappy about frequent inspections of his farms by officials from the Vaslui Veterinary and Food Safety Directorate, which he said had caused him financial losses. The same case also involves former deputy secretary general of the government Cristina Trăilă and former chairman of the PNL Vaslui branch Mihai Barbu. Both are suspected of arranging the meeting between Bolojan and Bogos. STUDENTS – In France, where student protests are expected to continue, more than 400 schools were closed on Friday, with classes held online. On Thursday, police made 2,000 arrests after students blocked access to schools, while at least two schools were set on fire. Protests by French school and university students have intensified, with further violence reported amid the involvement of far-left activists who are said by news agencies to have fuelled the unrest. More than 1,000 secondary schools have been affected, many of them suffering significant damage as a result of fires and vandalism. The anger among young people has caused disruption in several cities, bringing public transport to a standstill and damaging street furniture. The student movement began with the stated aim of calling for increased government funding for education, a less demanding curriculum and better conditions in schools and boarding facilities. “The violence that has taken place in schools and in their vicinity is extremely serious and goes far beyond issues concerning the education system. No grievance can justify such acts,” the French education minister said. DIASPORA – President Nicușor Dan has told Romanians living abroad that Romania has made progress over the past 20 years and urged them to consider returning home. Speaking in Bucharest at the ninth edition of the RePatriot Gala, the president stressed that the country needs a competitive and predictable business environment. RePatriot brings together more than 300 Romanian entrepreneurs, managers and professionals from the diaspora, selected for their achievements, contributions and impact in the countries where they live and work. On Friday, participants in the Black Sea resort of Mamaia, in south-eastern Romania, discussed Romania’s role on Europe’s front line of defence and developments in the Black Sea region, with a focus on security, energy, infrastructure, trade and technology. DRONE – Romania’s Defence Ministry said on Friday that another drone had crashed near the village of Plauru, in Tulcea County in south-eastern Romania, close to the country’s river border with Ukraine. The crash was followed by a fire, but there were no casualties or material damage, the ministry said. According to the ministry, an emergency response vehicle from the General Inspectorate for Emergencies(IGSU), along with Defence Ministry teams, was sent to the site to put out the fire. MILITARY – One of Europe’s largest interoperability exercises came to an end in Romania on Friday. According to the Romanian Gendarmerie, more than 500 soldiers and gendarmes from 19 countries across three continents took part in the drills. The military exercises, held from 27 September to 2 October, took place in four counties in southern Romania. The training included tactical simulations and troop movements.
